Chapter 1 – The University of Rhode Island Land Acknowledgement, Mission, Board of Trustees and the President of the University #22-23-2
The University of Rhode Island
1.10.10 Land Acknowledgement. “The University of Rhode Island occupies the traditional stomping ground of the Narragansett Nation and the Niantic People. We honor and respect the enduring and continuing relationship between the Indigenous peoples and this land by teaching and learning more about their history and present-day communities, and by becoming stewards of the land we, now too, inhabit.” #22-23-2

1.10.20 Background. The University of Rhode Island, the state’s land and sea grant research institution began as the state of Rhode Island’s Agricultural Experiment Station and agricultural school chartered in 1888. In 1892, the institution’s name was changed to the Rhode Island College of Agriculture and the Mechanic Arts. This name was subsequently changed to Rhode Island State College in 1909. The current name- the University of Rhode Island— was adopted in 1951 by an act of the State of Rhode Island’s General Assembly. For a complete history of the University, refer to https://www.uri.edu/about/history/.

1.10.30 Mission. The University of Rhode Island is the state’s flagship land and sea grant research institution, with a commitment to urban initiatives. A student-centered research institution, URI actively partners with other organizations globally and locally to advance knowledge and to develop informed residents and leaders. URI is committed to high-quality education, community engagement, and solving the world’s most important challenges. Situated on the traditional land and territories of the Narragansett Nation and the Niantic People, URI strives to create a diverse and inclusive environment for researchers, teachers, learners, and community members.
1.10.40 Values. The University of Rhode Island is committed to the following foundational values:
* Freedom to learn, teach, create, and conduct research with integrity in the pursuit and dissemination of new knowledge aimed at contributing to the public good.
* An inclusive, accessible, equitable and diverse community whereby we respect the rights and dignity of all.
* Intellectual curiosity, lifelong learning, leadership, and scholarship in creating a thriving URI community in service to Rhode Island and the world.

* and the chair of the Rhode Island Council on Postsecondary Education.
The members shall be appointed in accordance with R.I. Gen. Laws §16-32-2.2, which specifies that the governor will appoint the members with the advice and consent of the senate, and with due consideration to recommendations from the President of the University and the chair of the Board of Trustees.
At least three (3) of the members appointed by the governor shall be residents of the state of Rhode Island, at least one (1) of those members shall be selected after due consideration from a list of names of at least five (5) individuals submitted by the speaker of the house of representatives, and at least one (1) of those members shall be selected from a list of names of at least five (5) individuals submitted by the president of the senate.

The President of the University of Rhode Island will appoint one (1) faculty member and one (1) student member who shall be a full-time student in good standing at the University, and who shall both serve in non-voting, ex officio capacity for a single two (2) year term. A majority of voting members of the Board shall constitute a quorum and the vote of a majority of those present and voting shall be required for action.
A majority of the Board shall elect the chair of the Board from among the seventeen (17) voting board members pursuant to rules and regulations adopted by the Board establishing the procedure for electing a chair in accordance with R.I. Gen. Laws §16-32-2.2c.
In addition, the members of the Board shall elect a vice chair. The terms of office shall be three years or until a duly appointed successor is elected. Administrative Report January 2017, Administrative Report February 2021

1.30.10 Presidential Powers and Shared Governance. Per R.I. Gen. Laws §16 – 32 – 2.1, the President of the University shall have the following additional powers and duties:
* To create, and consolidate departments, divisions, programs, and courses of study within the university and the approved role and scope of the president’s authority adopted by the Board of trustees. Any new or proposed eliminations of departments, divisions, programs, or courses of study that are outside the role and scope approved by the Board shall require the review and approval of the Board;
* To adopt a budget for the university and submit to the Board of trustees for approval.
* To be responsible for the general management of property of the university.
* To recommend to the Board of trustees, tables of organization for the university.
* To submit to the Board of trustees and to compile and analyze institutional information for presentation to the Board annually. § R.I. Gen. Laws § 16-32-2.1.

Shared Governance - This presidential authority must be exercised “consistent with shared governance practices, [and] in conformity with R.I. Gen. Laws § 16-32-10,” which states that it “shall also be the duty of the president and a committee of the faculty, with the approval of the Board of trustees, to arrange courses of study conforming to all acts of Congress, and prescribe any qualifications for the admission of students and any rules of study, exercise, discipline, and government as the president and committee may deem proper.” The committee of the faculty to which this legislation refers has been and is understood to be the Faculty Senate of the University. CCJ 285 and CCJ 456 have been approved by the CCJ faculty as criminal justice elective options for majors and CCJ 334 has been approved as a criminology elective. CCJ 285 (Fac Sen Bill # 23-24-19) and 456 (Fac Sen Bill # 24-25-01) have been fully routed and approved through the curriculum process. BFA Theatre, Effective Fall 2025 Appendix B Changes approved for addition of THE200 to the curriculum per Faculty Senate Bill # 22-23-39A passed and signed by President on 23.04.20. This course (THE200) replaces two previous courses: THE291 (2 cr) and THE391 (2 cr). It is intended to make the production courses less complicated and confusing for students, allowing for consistency of the numbering system.

COLLEGE OF EDUCATION: BS Health & Physical Education, Effective Fall 2025 Appendix C Curricular changes are intended to align with national norms and availability of university course offerings.
The changes will offer students flexibility to select professional electives that closely align with their unique career goals in health and physical education.
COLLEGE OF THE ENVIRONMENT & LIFE SCIENCES: BS Geology & Geological Oceanography, Effective Fall 2025 Appendix D The current program has two options (Geology option and Geological Oceanography option).
We propose to add the Water and Climate Sciences as a third option.
The total number of credits in intro & professional courses, core geosciences and option specific courses, electives and supporting sciences is not changing, i.e. the number of credits will be comparable to the currently existing options.
However, option specific core course GEO 200, GEO 234 and GE0 280 replace GEO 210, GEO 320, GEO 370 and GEO 450.
Please refer to the advising sheet for the new Water and Climate Sciences option.
Copies of the existing (unchanged) advising sheet for the other two options are included for reference.

No new courses need to be created for the proposed changes.
Existing courses added to the revised core program are taught at a frequency that ensures degree completion in four years.
All existing classes have the capacity to accommodate additional inflow of students or, if needed, new class sections can be opened.
Students in the current options will not be affected by the proposed changes.
NEW SPECIALIZATIONS COLLEGE OF THE ENVIRONMENT & LIFE SCIENCES: Specialization in Water & Climate Science (BS Geology & Geological Oceanography), Effective Fall 2025 Appendix E The specialization in Water and Climate Sciences allows students the flexibility to define their own area of concentration within the water and climate sciences.
Example areas of concentration include environmental geology/ hydrogeology, and climate.
Students will be well prepared to pursue careers in environmental consulting, water resource management, sustainability initiatives, climate adaptation and resilience, and the emerging field of climate analytics.
These career opportunities are available with national and international government agencies, non-profit organizations, and the private sector.

The program will also equip students for research roles both in academia and the private sector.
Specialization Requirements: - All of the following courses: GEO200, GEO234G, GEO280, GEO305G, GEO483; GEO420 and/or GEO422; GEO482 and/or GEO484 - 24 credits of GEO courses at the 300-level or above

COLLEGE OF HEALTH SCIENCES: Specialization in Kinesiology (BS Kinesiology), Effective Fall 2025 Appendix F The Kinesiology Track provides flexibility to choose professional electives appropriate for a wide range of health and exercise science related careers. It is appropriate for students interested in pursuing health care professions such as physical therapy, chiropractic, medical doctor, or physician’s assistant or in becoming an exercise physiologist, strength and conditioning specialist, occupational therapist or health coach. Career opportunities exist in corporate, community, commercial and hospital-based fitness and wellness centers. The Kinesiology track will also prepare students for graduate study in clinical exercise physiology, cardiac rehabilitation, exercise science, health fitness, health promotion, preventive medicine and related fields. Kinesiology students will be prepared to become a certified professional in specialty areas including exercise physiology, strength and conditioning and/or personal training. The Kinesiology Track requirements include: 1. One of: PSY 200, STA 220, 307, or 308 2. 12 credits from the list of professional electives, with a minimum of 6 credits from KIN courses: CHM 105, 124, 126; CMB 210; EDC/HLT 401; KIN 125, 243, 369, 375G, 414, 425, 464G, 482; NUT 360; PSY 255. Other KIN or health-related courses may apply with approval from the KIN Department Chair. Additionally, there are free electives. The Department of Criminology and Criminal Justice offers a Bachelor of Arts (B.A.) degree.
The interdisciplinary degree in Criminology and Criminal Justice provides students with a wide range of course options so that students may tailor their learning to their educational and professional interests.
Our purpose is to empower our graduates to meaningfully consider, contribute to, and reimagine discourses and decisions about crime and justice.
The CCJ Department does this by making intentional choices about our work and remaining committed to continual professional growth and community building.
The program requires 30-49 credits in the major including CCJ/SOC 230(H) (with a grade of C or better), CCJ/PSC 274(H) (with a grade of C or better), and one of three capstone classes: CCJ 403, CCJ 410 or CCJ/PSC 476.
Students must select one research methods course from the following: ECN 306, PSC 310, PSY 200, or SOC 301.

Students are required to take six elective courses selected from the following two areas: criminology electives – AAF 230; CCJ 200 (approved topics), 334, 370, 400 (approved topics), 403, 410, 450, 476; AAF/HIS 366; PHL 318; PSY 254, 466; SOC 420; criminal justice electives – AAF 230; CCJ 200 (approved topics), 280, 285, 290,,, 332, 333, 381 (must be taken in combination with CHM 391 and/or ITR 305 for a total of 3 credits to count as 1 elective class), 456, 480, 490, 400 (approved topics), 403, 410, 476; CHM 391 (must either be repeated 3 times or taken in combination with CCJ 381 and/or ITR 305 for a total of 3 credits to count as 1 elective class); CCJ/HIS 361, AAF/HIS 366; ITR 305 (must be taken in combination with CHM 391 and/or CCJ 381 for a total of 3 credits to count as 1 elective class) PSC 334, 371, 388, 472; PSY 465; SOC 303.
At least two courses must be taken from each elective area and no more than four courses can be taken in either area.
All electives must be a minimum of 3 credits.
While CCJ 403, 410, and CCJ/PSC 476 are each capstone classes and electives, students may not use the same course to count as both a capstone and an elective class.

When appropriate, and by permission of the Department Chair, students may substitute internship credit (SOC 477, PSC 375/376, PSY 305, or GWS 300) or independent study credit (CCJ 485, SOC 498/499, PSC 455/456, PSY 489, or GWS 450) for one of their elective courses listed above.
No more than 3 credits may be used toward the major from internship or independent study.
Internal transfers into the CCJ major form a different major, or students wishing to add the CCJ major to their current major, must have a minimum 2.50 GPA.
A total of 120 credits is required for graduation.
At least 30 of these credits must be in courses at the 300-level or above.
In order to transfer into the criminology and criminal justice B.A. program from University College for Academic Success, a student must have completed at least 24 credits and have an earned a minimum of a 2.0 GPA.

Earth is rapidly changing changing, affecting the lives of everyone, including our students.
Reflecting these changes in the environment, interest is growing in the science of water and climate.
Our proposal addresses the need for a new option focused on these two important topics.
Therefore, the goal is to establish Water and Climate Sciences as an option under the existing major in Geology and Geological Oceanography - BS.

Successful geoscience programs will no doubt continue to include many core geoscience teachings, but they will also need to provide students with expertise in fields not necessarily recognized by incoming students as being part of the geosciences, such as water and climate sciences.
Further, an increasing need to analyze large datasets will require our students to obtain higher-level data skills for competing in the workforce.
